A eulogy is a formal, heartfelt speech — or sometimes a piece of writing — that praises and honors a person, most commonly someone who has recently died. It is delivered at a funeral, memorial service, or burial ceremony by someone who was close to the deceased: a spouse, a child, a best friend, a sibling, or a colleague. Sometimes a religious leader such as a priest or minister delivers it. The person who gives the eulogy is called a eulogist.

The whole purpose of a eulogy is to celebrate the life of someone who has passed away — to tell the people gathered in grief who that person truly was, what made them special, and why they will be remembered. Think of it this way: when someone you love dies, you want the world to know how wonderful they were. A eulogy is how you do that — through words, spoken with love, in front of people who shared in that love.

A good eulogy is deeply personal. It doesn't simply list facts about the person's life — that would feel cold and distant. Instead, it paints a living, breathing picture of who the person was through stories, personal memories, and observations. It might describe the person's character — their kindness, humor, generosity, or wisdom. It might include a specific story that captures exactly who they were at their best. It often speaks about their achievements, their relationships, and the lasting impact they had on the people around them. It closes with a final farewell — a tribute that gives the audience a sense of peace and closure.

The tone of a eulogy is solemn and respectful, because it is given at a time of deep grief. But it is also warm, loving, and celebratory — because it is about honoring a life fully lived, not just mourning its end. Eulogies often include light, gentle humor, because sharing a funny memory of someone is one of the most human ways of keeping their spirit alive in the room. A good eulogy doesn't only make people cry; it makes them feel genuinely grateful that the person existed at all.

While "eulogy" is most powerfully associated with funerals, the word can also be used in a broader sense to describe any formal, public expression of high praise for a person — even someone still alive. For example, at a professor's retirement ceremony, a student might deliver a eulogy in their honor. At a sports team's farewell dinner, a captain might give a eulogy for a beloved coach who is leaving. In this broader use, the word simply means a formal tribute of deep admiration. That said, this wider usage is far less common in everyday speech. When most people hear the word "eulogy," they immediately picture a funeral.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Three words are often confused with "eulogy," so it is worth knowing exactly how each one is different.

Obituary: An obituary is a short, factual written notice of someone's death, typically published in a newspaper or online. It covers the basic information: when and where the person was born, what they did for work, who their family members are, and when they died. It is informational rather than emotional. A eulogy, by contrast, is personal and heartfelt — it is spoken aloud and focuses on who the person was, not just the facts of their life.

Elegy: An elegy is a poem or song written in sorrow and mourning for someone who has died. Both elegies and eulogies honor the dead, but they are different in form and feeling. An elegy is a creative, artistic work driven largely by grief and sadness. A eulogy is a speech or prose tribute driven primarily by praise and celebration of the person's life.

Tribute: A tribute is a broad, general term for any expression of admiration, gratitude, or respect for someone. A eulogy is a type of tribute — a specific, formal one given in the context of death or a significant farewell. Every eulogy is a tribute, but not every tribute is a eulogy.

• She delivered a moving eulogy at her father's funeral that made everyone in the room both laugh and cry.
  • The president read a eulogy for the fallen soldiers at the national memorial ceremony.
  • The students surprised their retiring teacher with a eulogy that listed all the ways she had changed their lives.
  • He had been asked to write the eulogy for his best friend, and he sat for hours searching for words worthy of him.
The plural of eulogy is eulogies. For example: Three eulogies were read at the memorial service, each one revealing a different and equally beautiful side of the man everyone had loved.
A eulogy is a formal, heartfelt speech or written tribute that praises and honors a person's life, most commonly delivered at a funeral by someone who knew and deeply loved them.
